items.subject: eng

skill.th: สำนวน cross one's mind

topic.th: บทสนทนาในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
A: I heard you're thinking of leaving the school orchestra.
B: ______ I haven't made up my mind yet, though.

explanation.en: 'It has crossed my mind' means 'I have thought about it', which fits 'I haven't made up my mind yet'. 'I've changed my mind' suggests a decision has been made, 'it never crossed my mind' denies the rumour completely, and 'out of my mind' means crazy.
explanation.th: it has crossed my mind แปลว่าเคยคิดถึงเรื่องนี้อยู่ ซึ่งเข้ากับ 'ยังไม่ได้ตัดสินใจ' ส่วน I've changed my mind แสดงว่าตัดสินใจแล้ว it never crossed my mind คือปฏิเสธว่าไม่เคยคิดเลย และ out of my mind แปลว่าเสียสติ

choices: Well, it has crossed my mind.
Well, it never crossed my mind.
Well, I've changed my mind about it.
Well, it's out of my mind.

items.subject: eng

skill.en: Expressing doubt: I wouldn't count on it
skill.th: การแสดงความไม่มั่นใจ: I wouldn't count on it

topic.th: บทสนทนาในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
A: Do you think Ken will help us move house on Saturday?
B: ______ He's never once turned up when he said he would.

explanation.en: B's reason (Ken never turns up) shows doubt, so 'I wouldn't count on it' (don't rely on it) is right. The other three all express certainty that Ken will come.
explanation.th: เหตุผลของ B (เคนไม่เคยมาตามนัด) แสดงความสงสัย จึงใช้ I wouldn't count on it (อย่าหวังเลย) ส่วนอีกสามตัวเลือกแสดงความมั่นใจว่าเคนจะมา

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การขอให้พูดซ้ำและการตอบ

topic.th: บทสนทนาในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
A: Sorry, I didn't catch the last part. Could you run that by me again?
B: ______ I said the deadline has been moved forward to Friday.

explanation.en: 'Run that by me again' asks B to repeat, and B does repeat the information, so 'I'll go over it again' fits. 'Run after you' means chase, and 'catch it later' misuses A's word 'catch'.
explanation.th: run that by me again แปลว่าช่วยพูดอีกครั้ง และ B ก็พูดซ้ำจริง จึงตอบ I'll go over it again ส่วน run after you แปลว่าวิ่งตาม และ catch it later ใช้คำ catch ผิดความหมาย

choices: Sure, I'll go over it again.
No, I didn't say anything to you.

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การแสดงความไม่เห็นด้วยอย่างนุ่มนวล

topic.th: บทสนทนาในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
A: The new manager wants us to work every Saturday this month.
B: You're kidding! ______
A: I know. Most of us already have plans.

explanation.en: B is shocked ('You're kidding!') and A agrees with a complaint, so B must say the request is unreasonable: 'That's a bit much.' 'Right up my street' means exactly what I like, 'Fair play to her' praises the manager, and 'the least we can do' means it is a small effort.
explanation.th: B ตกใจ ('You're kidding!') และ A ตอบรับด้วยการบ่น แสดงว่า B มองว่าเกินไป จึงพูด That's a bit much ส่วน right up my street แปลว่าตรงกับที่ชอบ Fair play to her เป็นการชม และ the least we can do แปลว่าเป็นเรื่องเล็กน้อยที่ควรทำ

choices: That's a bit much, isn't it?
That sounds right up my street.
That's the least we can do.

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำปรากฏร่วม pose a threat

topic.th: คำปรากฏร่วมและกริยาวลี

items.stem: Rising sea levels ______ a serious threat to low-lying coastal cities such as Bangkok.

explanation.en: The collocation is 'pose a threat'. 'Raise' goes with questions or money, 'make up' means form or invent, and 'cause up' is not English.
explanation.th: คำปรากฏร่วมคือ pose a threat (เป็นภัยคุกคาม) ส่วน raise ใช้กับคำถามหรือเงิน make up แปลว่าประกอบเป็นหรือแต่งขึ้น และ cause up ไม่มีใช้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำนามที่สับสนง่าย

topic.th: คำศัพท์เชิงวิชาการ

items.stem: The two sides failed to reach a ______, so the talks were postponed until next month.

explanation.en: 'Reach a consensus' means come to general agreement. 'Consent' is permission, a 'census' counts the population, and 'conscience' is your sense of right and wrong.
explanation.th: reach a consensus แปลว่าได้ข้อตกลงร่วมกัน ส่วน consent แปลว่าการยินยอม census คือการสำมะโนประชากร และ conscience แปลว่ามโนธรรม

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำปรากฏร่วม shed light on

topic.th: คำปรากฏร่วมและกริยาวลี

items.stem: Her research ______ new light on the causes of coral bleaching in the Gulf of Thailand.

explanation.en: The idiom is 'shed light on' (help to explain). 'Put', 'make' and 'give' are not used with 'light on' in this meaning.
explanation.th: สำนวนคือ shed light on (ช่วยให้กระจ่าง) ไม่ใช้ put, make หรือ give ในความหมายนี้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: กริยาวลี cover up

topic.th: คำปรากฏร่วมและกริยาวลี

items.stem: Officials were accused of trying to ______ the scandal by destroying important documents.

explanation.en: To 'cover up' a scandal is to hide it, which matches destroying documents. 'Make up for' means compensate, 'look up to' means admire, and 'put up with' means tolerate.
explanation.th: cover up แปลว่าปกปิด ซึ่งเข้ากับการทำลายเอกสาร ส่วน make up for แปลว่าชดเชย look up to แปลว่านับถือ และ put up with แปลว่าทนต่อ

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำคุณศัพท์ที่สับสนง่าย: unfounded

topic.th: คำศัพท์เชิงวิชาการ

items.stem: The company's claims about its 'eco-friendly' packaging turned out to be completely ______; independent tests found no difference from ordinary plastic.

explanation.en: 'Unfounded' means not based on facts, which the tests showed. 'Unfunded' means without money, 'founding' relates to starting an organisation, and 'profound' means deep.
explanation.th: unfounded แปลว่าไม่มีมูลความจริง ซึ่งผลการทดสอบยืนยัน ส่วน unfunded แปลว่าไม่มีเงินทุน founding เกี่ยวกับการก่อตั้ง และ profound แปลว่าลึกซึ้ง

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การสร้างคำ comprehensive

topic.th: การสร้างคำ

items.stem: The museum has a ______ collection of Ayutthaya-period ceramics, unmatched anywhere else in the world.

explanation.en: A 'comprehensive' collection is complete and wide-ranging. 'Comprehensible' means easy to understand, 'comprehension' is a noun, and 'comprehending' means understanding.
explanation.th: comprehensive แปลว่าครอบคลุมครบถ้วน ส่วน comprehensible แปลว่าเข้าใจได้ comprehension เป็นคำนาม และ comprehending แปลว่ากำลังเข้าใจ

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำคุณศัพท์เชิงวิชาการจากความขัดแย้งในประโยค

topic.th: คำศัพท์เชิงวิชาการ

items.stem: Although the evidence against him was largely ______, the jury found it convincing enough to convict him.

explanation.en: 'Although' needs a contrast with 'convincing enough to convict': circumstantial evidence suggests guilt indirectly, so it is normally weaker. 'Conclusive' and 'substantial' evidence would not create a contrast, and 'superstitious' does not describe evidence.
explanation.th: Although ต้องการความขัดแย้งกับ 'น่าเชื่อพอจะตัดสินลงโทษ' หลักฐานแวดล้อม (circumstantial) บ่งชี้ทางอ้อมจึงมักอ่อนกว่า ส่วน conclusive และ substantial ไม่ทำให้เกิดความขัดแย้ง และ superstitious ใช้กับหลักฐานไม่ได้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ความหมายของคำคุณศัพท์จากบริบท: ambiguous

topic.th: คำศัพท์เชิงวิชาการ

items.stem: The minister's speech was deliberately ______, allowing both supporters and critics to interpret it however they wished.

explanation.en: A speech that can be interpreted in different ways is 'ambiguous'. 'Explicit' means clear and direct (the opposite), 'ambitious' means aiming high, and 'unanimous' means agreed by everyone.
explanation.th: สุนทรพจน์ที่ตีความได้หลายแบบคือ ambiguous (กำกวม) ส่วน explicit แปลว่าชัดเจนตรงไปตรงมา (ตรงข้าม) ambitious แปลว่าทะเยอทะยาน และ unanimous แปลว่าเป็นเอกฉันท์

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การสลับที่: Little did …

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Little ______ that the decision would change her life for ever.

explanation.en: Negative adverbs such as 'little' at the start of a sentence require inversion: 'Little did she know'.
explanation.th: คำกริยาวิเศษณ์เชิงปฏิเสธ เช่น little เมื่ออยู่ต้นประโยคต้องสลับที่ จึงเป็น Little did she know

items.subject: eng

skill.th: whose ที่ใช้กับสิ่งของ

topic.th: อนุประโยคและคำเชื่อม

items.stem: The report, ______ conclusions were widely criticised, was eventually withdrawn.

explanation.en: 'Whose' shows possession and can refer to things: the report's conclusions → whose conclusions. 'Which conclusions' and 'its conclusions' cannot introduce this clause, and 'that' is not used after a comma.
explanation.th: whose แสดงความเป็นเจ้าของและใช้กับสิ่งของได้ (the report's conclusions → whose conclusions) ส่วน which และ its ใช้นำอนุประโยคนี้ไม่ได้ และ that ใช้หลังจุลภาคไม่ได้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: อนุประโยค past participle

topic.th: อนุประโยคและคำเชื่อม

items.stem: ______ in the thirteenth century, the temple is one of the oldest buildings in the province.

explanation.en: The temple was built by others, so a passive participle clause is needed: 'Built in the thirteenth century, …'. 'Building' and 'Having built' would mean the temple did the building.
explanation.th: วัดถูกสร้างโดยผู้อื่น จึงต้องใช้ past participle ในความหมาย passive คือ Built … ส่วน Building และ Having built แปลว่าวัดเป็นผู้สร้าง

items.subject: eng

skill.th: future perfect continuous

topic.th: กาล (Tense)

items.stem: By this time next year, Somchai ______ at the university for six months.

explanation.en: 'By this time next year … for six months' measures the duration of an action up to a point in the future: future perfect continuous.
explanation.th: 'By this time next year … for six months' บอกระยะเวลาของการกระทำจนถึงจุดหนึ่งในอนาคต จึงใช้ future perfect continuous

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำเชื่อมคู่ not … but …

topic.th: อนุประโยคและคำเชื่อม

items.stem: It was not the price ______ the poor service that made customers stop coming.

explanation.en: 'Not X but Y' corrects a wrong idea: the cause was the service, not the price.
explanation.th: not X but Y ใช้แก้ความเข้าใจผิด คือสาเหตุไม่ใช่ราคาแต่เป็นการบริการ

items.subject: eng

skill.th: เงื่อนไขแบบที่ 3 แบบสลับที่

topic.th: ประโยคเงื่อนไขและ wish

items.stem: ______ the instructions more carefully, he would not have broken the machine.

explanation.en: 'Would not have broken' is a third-conditional result, so the condition must be past perfect. Without 'if', it is inverted: 'Had he read'.
explanation.th: would not have broken เป็นผลของเงื่อนไขแบบที่ 3 เงื่อนไขจึงต้องเป็น past perfect และเมื่อละ if ต้องสลับที่เป็น Had he read

items.subject: eng

skill.th: passive ของกริยารายงาน + perfect infinitive

topic.th: ประโยค passive

items.stem: The suspect is believed ______ the country last week, shortly before the police arrived.

explanation.en: The belief is now, but the leaving happened earlier (last week), so the perfect infinitive is needed: 'is believed to have left'.
explanation.th: ความเชื่อเกิดขึ้นตอนนี้ แต่การออกนอกประเทศเกิดก่อนหน้า (สัปดาห์ที่แล้ว) จึงต้องใช้ perfect infinitive คือ is believed to have left

items.subject: eng

skill.th: เงื่อนไขแบบทางการ: were … to

topic.th: ประโยคเงื่อนไขและ wish

items.stem: Were the government ______ taxes on sugar, the price of soft drinks would rise sharply.

explanation.en: 'Were + subject + to-infinitive' is a formal inverted form of 'If the government raised …'.
explanation.th: Were + ประธาน + to-infinitive เป็นรูปสลับที่แบบทางการของ If the government raised …

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ความสอดคล้องหลัง one of those who

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: She is one of those people who ______ always complaining about something.

explanation.en: 'Who' refers to 'those people' (plural), not to 'one', so the verb is 'are'.
explanation.th: who แทน those people ซึ่งเป็นพหูพจน์ ไม่ได้แทน one กริยาจึงต้องเป็น are

items.subject: eng

skill.th: would sooner … than + infinitive ไม่มี to

topic.th: รูปแบบกริยา (gerund/infinitive)

items.stem: I'd sooner walk home than ______ for a taxi in this rain.

explanation.en: 'Would sooner/rather do X than do Y' uses the bare infinitive in both parts.
explanation.th: would sooner/rather do X than do Y ใช้ infinitive ไม่มี to ทั้งสองส่วน

items.subject: eng

skill.th: reach a decision (ไม่ใช้บุพบท)

topic.th: รูปแบบกริยา (gerund/infinitive)

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The committee spent three hours [[discussing]] the proposal [[without]] [[reaching]] [[to]] a decision.

explanation.en: 'Reach' is transitive: we 'reach a decision', not 'reach to a decision'. (Note also 'discuss' with no 'about'.)
explanation.th: reach เป็นกริยาที่ตามด้วยกรรมโดยตรง ใช้ reach a decision ไม่ใช่ reach to a decision

items.subject: eng

skill.th: participle clause แสดงผล

topic.th: อนุประโยคและคำเชื่อม

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: Scarcely [[had]] the plane taken off [[when]] one of the engines [[caught]] fire, [[forced]] the pilot to return.

explanation.en: The last part shows the result of the fire and needs an active present participle: '…caught fire, forcing the pilot to return'.
explanation.th: ส่วนท้ายแสดงผลของไฟไหม้ ต้องใช้ present participle แบบ active คือ … caught fire, forcing the pilot to return

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำนามนับไม่ได้ information

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[Informations]] about the course [[is]] available [[on]] the school's [[website]].

explanation.en: 'Information' is uncountable and has no plural form; the verb 'is' is correct for it.
explanation.th: information เป็นคำนามนับไม่ได้ ไม่มีรูปพหูพจน์ และกริยา is ถูกต้องแล้ว

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ความสอดคล้องกับ along with

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The professor, [[along with]] her students, [[are]] [[travelling]] to the conference [[by]] train.

explanation.en: Phrases such as 'along with' or 'as well as' do not change the subject. The subject is 'the professor', so the verb is 'is'.
explanation.th: วลี along with หรือ as well as ไม่ได้ทำให้ประธานเปลี่ยน ประธานคือ the professor กริยาจึงต้องเป็น is

items.subject: eng

skill.th: fewer กับ less

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[Less]] students applied this year [[than]] last year, [[so]] the school [[extended]] the deadline.

explanation.en: 'Students' is a plural countable noun, so it takes 'fewer', not 'less'.
explanation.th: students เป็นคำนามนับได้พหูพจน์ จึงต้องใช้ fewer ไม่ใช่ less

items.subject: eng

skill.th: would rather … than + infinitive ไม่มี to

topic.th: รูปแบบกริยา (gerund/infinitive)

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: She would rather [[stay]] at home tonight [[than]] [[going]] to the party, [[which]] starts very late.

explanation.en: After 'would rather … than' both verbs take the bare infinitive: 'than go to the party'.
explanation.th: หลัง would rather … than กริยาทั้งสองต้องเป็น infinitive ไม่มี to จึงต้องเป็น than go

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำนามพหูพจน์หลัง a number of

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The research team [[has made]] [[a number of]] important [[discovery]] [[over]] the past decade.

explanation.en: 'A number of' is followed by a plural noun: 'a number of important discoveries'.
explanation.th: a number of ต้องตามด้วยคำนามพหูพจน์ คือ a number of important discoveries

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การสลับที่หลัง Never before

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[Never before]] [[the city has seen]] such a large protest, [[and]] the police [[were]] unprepared.

explanation.en: A negative adverbial at the start of the sentence requires inversion: 'Never before had the city seen …' (past perfect, since the police were unprepared at that past time).
explanation.th: คำกริยาวิเศษณ์เชิงปฏิเสธที่ต้นประโยคต้องสลับที่ คือ Never before had the city seen … (ใช้ past perfect เพราะตำรวจไม่พร้อมในเวลานั้นในอดีต)

items.subject: eng

skill.th: present perfect แบบ passive

topic.th: ประโยค passive

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The warning system, [[which]] was installed in 2006, [[has]] [[been improving]] several times [[since then]].

explanation.en: The system does not improve itself; engineers improve it, and 'several times' counts completed actions. It should be passive: 'has been improved'.
explanation.th: ระบบไม่ได้ปรับปรุงตัวเอง แต่ถูกวิศวกรปรับปรุง และ several times นับการกระทำที่เสร็จแล้ว จึงต้องใช้ passive คือ has been improved

items.subject: eng

skill.th: It's no use + V-ing

topic.th: รูปแบบกริยา (gerund/infinitive)

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[It's]] no use [[to argue]] with him; he [[never]] changes his mind [[once]] it is made up.

explanation.en: The fixed expression 'It's no use' is followed by the -ing form: 'It's no use arguing with him'.
explanation.th: สำนวน It's no use ต้องตามด้วย V-ing คือ It's no use arguing with him

items.subject: eng

skill.th: วลีตายตัว in danger of

topic.th: เติมคำในบทความ

items.passage: Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that around half are (1) ______ danger of disappearing by the end of this century. A language rarely dies suddenly. (2) ______, it fades over several generations, as parents who speak it at home decide that their children's future lies in a more widely used language. items.passage:
For most of the history of medicine, the placebo — a treatment with no active ingredient — was regarded as a nuisance. In clinical trials it existed only to be beaten: a new drug was considered effective if patients who received it improved more than those given sugar pills. That patients on placebo often improved too was treated as background noise, a statistical problem to be subtracted.

Over the past few decades, however, researchers have begun to take that noise seriously. Brain-imaging studies have shown that when people in pain receive a placebo they believe to be a painkiller, their brains release natural pain-relieving chemicals. The improvement, in other words, is not merely imagined; it has a measurable physical basis. The size of the effect also depends on details that have nothing to do with chemistry. Two pills tend to work better than one, injections better than pills, and expensive placebos better than cheap ones. Even the colour of a tablet can influence how patients describe its effects.

What these findings suggest is that the experience of being treated — the ritual of the consultation, the confidence of the doctor, the expectation of relief — is itself a kind of treatment. This helps to explain a puzzling observation: in some trials of treatments for pain, the effect of placebo appears to have grown stronger over the years, particularly in countries where advertising has made patients more familiar with the idea of medicines that work.

The obvious ethical difficulty is deception. A doctor who prescribes a sugar pill while claiming it is a powerful drug is lying to the patient, and most medical codes forbid this. Surprisingly, though, deception may not always be necessary. In a number of small studies, patients with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome were given pills openly labelled as placebos and told honestly that they contained no medicine. Many still reported significant improvement compared with patients who received no pills at all.

These 'open-label' results should be treated with caution. The studies were small, and symptoms such as pain and tiredness are partly subjective, which makes them especially sensitive to expectation. No one suggests that a placebo can shrink a tumour or cure an infection. But the research has shifted the question that doctors ask. Instead of asking only which chemical a patient needs, they are beginning to ask how the way treatment is delivered might make every medicine, real or not, work a little better.
items.stem: What is the main point of the passage?

explanation.en: The passage moves from the old view (a nuisance, 'noise') to evidence that the effect is physical, and ends with how this changes the questions doctors ask. It never claims placebos beat real drugs.

For most of the history of medicine, the placebo — a treatment with no active ingredient — was regarded as a nuisance. In clinical trials it existed only to be beaten: a new drug was considered effective if patients who received it improved more than those given sugar pills. That patients on placebo often improved too was treated as background noise, a statistical problem to be subtracted.

Over the past few decades, however, researchers have begun to take that noise seriously. Brain-imaging studies have shown that when people in pain receive a placebo they believe to be a painkiller, their brains release natural pain-relieving chemicals. The improvement, in other words, is not merely imagined; it has a measurable physical basis. The size of the effect also depends on details that have nothing to do with chemistry. Two pills tend to work better than one, injections better than pills, and expensive placebos better than cheap ones. Even the colour of a tablet can influence how patients describe its effects.

What these findings suggest is that the experience of being treated — the ritual of the consultation, the confidence of the doctor, the expectation of relief — is itself a kind of treatment. This helps to explain a puzzling observation: in some trials of treatments for pain, the effect of placebo appears to have grown stronger over the years, particularly in countries where advertising has made patients more familiar with the idea of medicines that work.

items.passage:
The letter arrived on the morning my grandfather turned eighty, which my mother later said was either a coincidence or the cruellest joke the post office had ever played. It was addressed to him in careful, old-fashioned handwriting, and the stamp was from a country he had not visited for sixty years.

He did not open it at breakfast. He placed it beside his plate, squared its edges with the side of his hand, and went on eating his rice porridge as though it were an ordinary bill. My cousins and I, who had been told almost nothing about his life before he came to Thailand, exchanged glances across the table. My aunt asked, in the bright voice she used for difficult subjects, whether he was going to read it. 'Later,' he said, and that was the end of the conversation.

Later turned out to be three days. In that time the envelope moved from the dining table to the shelf above his radio, and from there to the pocket of the cardigan he wore in the garden regardless of the heat. I began to understand that he was not ignoring it. He was keeping it close in the way you might keep a stone that is too hot to hold, waiting for it to cool.

On the fourth evening he called me into his room. He was sitting on the edge of the bed with the letter open on his knee, and his glasses had slipped down his nose. 'My eyes are tired,' he said, which I knew was not true; he read the newspaper every morning without difficulty. 'Read it to me.'

The letter was from a woman named Hana, the younger sister of a boy he had gone to school with. Her brother had died that spring. Among his things she had found a photograph of two boys on a bridge, and on the back, in her brother's writing, my grandfather's name and the words: 'I should have gone with him.' She did not know what it meant, she wrote, but she thought he should have it.

When I finished, my grandfather took the photograph from the envelope and looked at it for a long time. Then he said something I have thought about ever since. 'All these years I believed he was angry with me for leaving. It never occurred to me that he might have envied me.' He laughed softly, wiped his eyes with the back of his wrist, and asked me to fetch a pen.

explanation.en: The letter, which brought news of a death and an old regret, arrived on his eightieth birthday — a celebration spoiled by sad news, which is why the timing seemed cruel.

The grandfather disliked celebrating his birthday.
The post office often delivered letters late.

Walk through the galleries of almost any major European museum and you will find objects that left their countries of origin under questionable circumstances: bronze sculptures removed by soldiers, stone carvings bought from officials who had no right to sell them, sacred objects taken from temples during periods of colonial rule. For decades, museums have resisted requests to return such items. Their arguments deserve to be heard, but I believe that, in most cases, they no longer hold.

The first argument is that these objects are safer where they are. Museums in wealthy countries, the claim goes, have the climate control, security and expert staff needed to preserve fragile works. This may once have been true, but it is increasingly difficult to defend. Many countries that have requested returns now have modern museums of their own, and some of the objects in question have been damaged in Western collections through poor storage or careless restoration. More fundamentally, the argument assumes that the original owners cannot be trusted with their own heritage — an assumption with an uncomfortable history.

A second argument holds that great 'universal' museums allow visitors to compare civilisations side by side, and that dispersing their collections would destroy this. It is a genuinely attractive idea. Yet the universal museum is universal mainly for those who can travel to London, Paris or Berlin. For a student in Lagos or Phnom Penh, the most important objects from her own country's past may be thousands of kilometres away, and far more expensive for her to see than for a tourist from the city where they are kept.

The third argument is practical: if one object is returned, the museum will face endless demands, and its collections will be emptied. This fear seems exaggerated. Requests are generally made for a limited number of objects of special cultural or religious importance, not for every pot and coin. Moreover, return need not mean an end to cooperation. Several recent agreements have combined the transfer of ownership with long-term loans, joint research and exchanges of exhibitions.

None of this means that every claim is straightforward. Ownership can be genuinely unclear, especially when borders and states have changed, and each case requires careful research. But the burden of proof should lie with the museums. When an object was clearly taken by force or without the consent of those who owned it, the question should not be whether it can be returned, but how and when.
